title: 1 Kings 21:1–16
context: Naboth refuses to sell Ahab his family inheritance out of reverence for the LORD. Jezebel, in Ahab’s name, arranges a fast, false witnesses, and Naboth’s stoning, and Ahab takes possession of the vineyard. The guilt lies with Jezebel, Ahab, and those who carried out the plot, not with Naboth.

verses.text: After these things, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard which was in Jezreel, next to the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: Naboth the Jezreelite has a vineyard in Jezreel next to Ahab’s palace. Arminian readers see the stage set for a conflict between royal desire and an ordinary Israelite’s rights.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrator establishing Naboth’s legitimate ownership. The vineyard’s location beside the palace explains Ahab’s interest without excusing what follows.

verses.text: Ahab spoke to Naboth, saying, “Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a garden of herbs, because it is near my house; and I will give you for it a better vineyard than it. Or, if it seems good to you, I will give you its worth in money.”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab says, “Give me your vineyard … I will give you for it a better vineyard than it,” or money. Arminian readers see an offer that appears fair on the surface.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a seemingly reasonable request. Readers in this tradition note that the offer, however polite, does not account for the covenant meaning of the land as Naboth understands it.

verses.text: Naboth said to Ahab, “May the LORD forbid me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you!”
verses.arminianNotes: Naboth says, “May the LORD forbid me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you!” Arminian readers see faithful conviction rooted in God’s law about family inheritance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Naboth honoring God’s ordering of the land, reflected in passages such as Leviticus 25:23 and Numbers 36:7. Naboth bears no blame for refusing; he acts out of reverence for the LORD.

verses.text: Ahab came into his house sullen and angry because of the word which Naboth the Jezreelite had spoken to him, for he had said, “I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers.” He laid himself down on his bed, and turned away his face, and would eat no bread.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab goes home “sullen and angry,” lies down, turns away his face, and eats no bread. Arminian readers see a king sulking because a faithful man refused him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ahab’s self-pity. The narrator shows Ahab knowing Naboth’s reason and choosing resentment, which opens the way for Jezebel’s scheme.

verses.text: But Jezebel his wife came to him, and said to him, “Why is your spirit so sad that you eat no bread?”
verses.arminianNotes: Jezebel asks, “Why is your spirit so sad that you eat no bread?” Arminian readers see her noticing Ahab’s mood and preparing to act on it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Jezebel entering the story decisively. Her question leads to Ahab’s retelling, which shapes how she responds.

verses.text: He said to her, “Because I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite, and said to him, ‘Give me your vineyard for money; or else, if it pleases you, I will give you another vineyard for it.’ He answered, ‘I will not give you my vineyard.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Ahab recounts the exchange but omits Naboth’s appeal to “the inheritance of my fathers.” Arminian readers see a selective retelling that removes the covenant reason for Naboth’s refusal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ahab framing Naboth as simply unwilling. Readers in this tradition note the omission, though the text does not state Ahab’s purpose in leaving it out.

verses.text: Jezebel his wife said to him, “Do you now govern the kingdom of Israel? Arise, and eat bread, and let your heart be merry. I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jezebel says, “Do you now govern the kingdom of Israel? … I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.” Arminian readers see her contempt for limits on royal power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Jezebel asserting a view of kingship that ignores God’s law. Her promise sets in motion the plot that leads to Naboth’s murder.

verses.text: So she wrote letters in Ahab’s name and sealed them with his seal, and sent the letters to the elders and to the nobles who were in his city, who lived with Naboth.
verses.arminianNotes: Jezebel writes letters in Ahab’s name, seals them with his seal, and sends them to Naboth’s elders and nobles. Arminian readers see her using royal authority deliberately to plan a crime.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Jezebel orchestrating the plot through official channels. The use of Ahab’s seal also implicates Ahab in what is done in his name.

verses.text: She wrote in the letters, saying, “Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people.
verses.arminianNotes: She writes, “Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people.” Arminian readers see religious ritual twisted to give a murder the appearance of legitimacy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a fast misused to stage a false trial. Readers in this tradition note how outward piety is exploited for injustice.

verses.text: Set two men, wicked fellows, before him, and let them testify against him, saying, ‘You cursed God and the king!’ Then carry him out, and stone him to death.”
verses.arminianNotes: She instructs them to set “two men, wicked fellows” to testify, “You cursed God and the king!” and then to stone him. Arminian readers see deliberate false witness, forbidden in Exodus 20:16.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Jezebel plainly planning murder through perjury. The requirement of two witnesses in Deuteronomy 17:6 is manipulated to make the killing appear lawful.

verses.text: The men of his city, even the elders and the nobles who lived in his city, did as Jezebel had instructed them in the letters which she had written and sent to them.
verses.arminianNotes: The elders and nobles do “as Jezebel had instructed them.” Arminian readers see local leaders sharing responsibility by carrying out an unjust order.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the complicity of those who obeyed. The narrator names Jezebel’s instructions directly, leaving no doubt about who designed the crime.

verses.text: They proclaimed a fast, and set Naboth on high among the people.
verses.arminianNotes: They proclaim a fast and set Naboth on high. Arminian readers see the plan carried out exactly, highlighting the cold deliberateness of the conspiracy against an innocent man.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the staged proceedings unfold. The repetition of Jezebel’s words emphasizes that every step followed her design.

verses.text: The two men, the wicked fellows, came in and sat before him. The wicked fellows testified against him, even against Naboth, in the presence of the people, saying, “Naboth cursed God and the king!” Then they carried him out of the city and stoned him to death with stones.
verses.arminianNotes: The wicked fellows testify, “Naboth cursed God and the king!” and Naboth is stoned to death. Arminian readers see an innocent man killed through lies, with no fault of his own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a grave injustice. The narrative calls the witnesses “wicked fellows,” making clear that the charge was false and Naboth was innocent.

verses.text: Then they sent to Jezebel, saying, “Naboth has been stoned and is dead.”
verses.arminianNotes: They report to Jezebel, “Naboth has been stoned and is dead.” Arminian readers see the conspirators answering to the one who ordered the killing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Jezebel as the one directing the crime. The report confirms that she was the authority behind the murder.

verses.text: When Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, Jezebel said to Ahab, “Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he refused to give you for money; for Naboth is not alive, but dead.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jezebel tells Ahab, “Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite … for Naboth is not alive, but dead.” Arminian readers see her callous satisfaction in the result of her plot.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Jezebel presenting the murder as a gift to the king. Her words show no regard for the life taken or for God’s law.

verses.text: When Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, Ahab rose up to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, to take possession of it.
verses.arminianNotes: When Ahab hears Naboth is dead, he goes down to take possession of the vineyard. Arminian readers see Ahab accepting the fruit of the crime without protest, sharing in its guilt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ahab’s complicity. Readers in this tradition note that Ahab’s eager possession makes him responsible alongside Jezebel, as the LORD’s word will declare.
